aireadiness.q: Which set lists the five readiness dimensions taught in this topic?
options: Budget, headcount, vendors, timeline, hardware
Data, people, process, platform, risk
Models, prompts, evals, costs, latency
Sales, marketing, support, finance, legal
aireadiness.why: Readiness asks whether the data, people, process, platform and risk controls are in place. Model and cost questions come later, once a use case is chosen.

aireadiness.q: On a value versus effort 2x2, which box usually holds the best first pilot?
options: High value, low effort
High value, high effort
Low value, low effort
Low value, high effort
aireadiness.why: A quick win (high value, low effort) proves results fast and builds trust. Big bets are better once access, platform and trust exist.

aireadiness.q: A CEO at Harwick Tiles says 'we need AI' but names no problem. What do you do first?
options: Build a demo chatbot on their website that week
Run a readiness check and a use-case workshop with the people who do the work
Send a price list for your largest platform package
Ask IT to open access to every database
aireadiness.why: You need specific use cases with users, volume and a baseline before building anything. A demo without a problem rarely leads to a funded pilot.

aireadiness.q: The top-scored idea has data availability scored 1: the records are on paper in a warehouse. What is the best move?
options: Pilot it anyway since it scored highest on value
Drop it from the list forever
Pick the next quick win for the pilot and put digitising the data on the roadmap
Raise its data score to 3 so it qualifies
aireadiness.why: Data availability acts as a gate. Keep the idea, plan the data work with an owner, and pilot something that can start now.

aireadiness.q: Spot the mistake: 'Our roadmap starts eight pilots in parallel in Q1 so every department gets something.'
options: Nothing, parallel pilots finish faster
Eight is too few for a large company
Pilots should always last at least a year
A first customer rarely has owners, data access and attention for eight pilots at once
aireadiness.why: Too many parallel pilots spread owners and access thin, so most stall. Stage the roadmap and tie later pilots to results from the first.

options: Engineers running unit tests before each commit
Business users testing realistic tasks and formally accepting the system
Security staff scanning the system for weak points
A load test that checks peak traffic
golive.why: UAT is done by the customer's users on realistic work, and ends with a written sign-off. Unit, security and load tests are important but answer different questions.

golive.q: What is the main purpose of a go/no-go meeting?
options: To celebrate the launch with the sponsor
To plan next year's roadmap
For named owners to confirm agreed criteria are met before cutover
To write the UAT scripts
golive.why: Go/no-go is a decision against criteria set in advance, such as UAT signed and rollback tested. The result can be go, go with accepted risks, or no-go.

golive.q: Your dry-run migration at Halvard Clinics takes 9 hours but the cutover window is 5 hours. What is the best fix?
options: Ask for a bigger window only on the night
Load history the week before and move only recent changes (a delta) at cutover
Skip reconciliation to save time
Migrate half the data and add the rest later by hand
golive.why: Splitting into a history load and a delta load fits the window without dropping checks. Skipping reconciliation removes the proof the data is right.

golive.q: At the go/no-go, UAT is signed but the rollback has never been tried. What should you say?
options: Go, since UAT is signed
Go, and test the rollback if something breaks
Rollbacks are optional for AI systems
No-go or go-with-risk only if the sponsor accepts it; better to test the rollback in staging first
golive.why: An untested rollback may not work when you need it. Test it in staging, or at least have the sponsor accept the risk in writing.

golive.q: Spot the mistake: 'Staging passed, so production will work. We tested with the vendor's own test login.'
options: Staging should never be used before production
Staging may differ from production, such as a different identity provider, so check real sign-in
Nothing is wrong with this reasoning
Production must always be tested before staging
golive.why: Staging is often not a perfect copy. Differences in sign-in, network rules or data volume are common causes of go-live day failures.

supportops.q: In a typical support model, what does L2 do?
options: Investigates harder problems: logs, configuration, data, reproduction
Answers only password resets
Writes new product features
Signs the support contract
supportops.why: L1 handles known answers, L2 investigates and fixes configuration or data, and L3 changes code.

supportops.q: What does a first-response SLA promise?
options: The problem will be fully fixed within that time
A person will acknowledge the ticket and start work within that time
The customer gets a refund if unhappy
The ticket will be closed within one day
supportops.why: First response is about acknowledgement and starting work. Resolution targets, if any, are separate promises.

supportops.q: A user at Dunmore Bank writes 'the assistant is broken'. What do you ask first?
options: Whether they have tried a different browser
For their manager's name
Who is affected, exact steps, the output they saw, and the conversation ID
Whether they want a refund
supportops.why: You need facts to reproduce the issue: scope, steps, actual output and an ID to find it in logs.

supportops.q: Half of last month's tickets were 'how do I export a report'. What is the best next step?
options: Hire two more L2 engineers
Escalate it to L3 as a severity 1 bug
Ignore it because it is not a bug
Write a clear KB article and put it in the ticket form and L1 scripts
supportops.why: A repeat how-to question is a deflection opportunity. A short article where users look removes most of those tickets.

supportops.q: Spot the mistake: 'Hypercare ends when the FDE starts the next project.'
options: Hypercare should end when agreed exit criteria are met, such as no open Sev 1-2 and SLAs met
Hypercare should never end
Hypercare should end on go-live day
Nothing is wrong; that is the normal rule
supportops.why: Tying the end to the FDE's calendar leaves the customer without trained support. Exit criteria agreed at go-live make the handover safe.

incidents.q: During an incident, what is the incident commander's main job?
options: Debug the code personally
Coordinate the response, assign work and make decisions
Write the post-mortem only
Talk only to the press
incidents.why: The IC keeps the whole picture and decides. If the IC is debugging, nobody is coordinating.

incidents.q: A release went out at 09:30 and errors started at 09:32. What should you usually do first?
options: Spend an hour finding the exact line of code
Wait to see if it fixes itself
Roll back the release or turn off the feature to stop the harm
Email all users an apology
incidents.why: Stabilise first. Rolling back a recent change is often the fastest way to stop harm and also tests whether it caused the problem.

incidents.q: You promised a Sev 1 update at 11:00 but have no news. What do you do?
options: Wait until you have news
Send an update saying the status is unchanged, what you are trying, and the next update time
Ask the customer to stop asking
Close the incident
incidents.why: Keeping the timer builds trust. An update with no news but a clear next time is better than silence.

incidents.q: Evidence shows the customer's firewall change broke your product. What is the best approach?
options: Announce on the bridge that it is their fault
Refuse to help because it is not your code
Share the evidence as a shared problem, help them fix it, and look for what your product could do better
Hide the evidence to avoid conflict
incidents.why: Blame slows the fix. Evidence plus help fixes it fastest, and your product can usually fail more gracefully too.

incidents.q: Spot the mistake in this review action: 'The team should be more careful with releases.'
options: It has no single owner, no date and no way to check it is done
It is too specific
Actions should never mention releases
Nothing is wrong with it
incidents.why: Useful actions are concrete, owned by one person, dated and checkable, such as adding a test or an alert.

enablement.q: What is the main difference between training and enablement?
options: Training is online and enablement is in person
Enablement is the whole system of skills, materials and help, judged by what people can do later
Enablement is only for admins
There is no difference
enablement.why: Training is one activity. Enablement includes materials, help channels, champions and measuring behaviour weeks later.

enablement.q: Users at Pellbrook Clinic accept every date the assistant gives. What should you teach?
options: Never to use the assistant
That the model is always right with dates
How transformers work inside
Calibrated trust: always check dates and numbers against the source, with the source shown
enablement.why: Dates and numbers are a known weak spot. A simple check rule plus visible sources builds calibrated trust.

enablement.q: Which prompt library entry is most useful?
options: A tested prompt for a real task with an example, a check step and an owner
A list of general tips such as 'be specific'
A prompt copied from a public website
A prompt with real client names left in
enablement.why: Entries tied to real tasks, with examples, checks and an owner, get used and stay accurate. Confidential text must be removed.

enablement.q: A new AI Center of Excellence has a charter but no owner, budget or intake form. What will probably happen?
options: It will approve many useful projects
It will replace IT
It becomes a meeting with no output while people use tools without oversight
It will train every user automatically
enablement.why: A CoE needs a lead with time, a simple intake process and published decisions to have any effect.

enablement.q: Spot the mistake: 'Enablement succeeded because 95% of staff attended training.'
options: Attendance should be 100%
Attendance does not show skill; measure task checks, weekly use and output quality
Training should never be measured
Nothing is wrong
enablement.why: Attendance is easy to count but shows nothing about behaviour. Measure what people can do and how they use the tool.
